explanation: It's a double whammy: the heavy uterus slows down blood flow from the lower body, and pushing hard due to constipation makes those sensitive veins swell up. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T4#GNS121_U7_T4_h4)

question: What effect does progesterone have on the gallbladder during pregnancy?

options.A: It causes sluggish emptying and bile stasis
options.B: It stops the liver from producing cholesterol
options.C: It causes the gallbladder to shrink significantly
options.D: It speeds up the release of concentrated bile

explanation: Just like the gut, the gallbladder muscles relax too. This makes it empty slower, leaving bile sitting inside longer (stasis). [learn more](GNS121_U7_T4#GNS121_U7_T4_h5)

question: Why is there a higher risk of developing gallstones during pregnancy?

options.A: The growing uterus crushes the bile duct and blocks fluid flow
options.B: The liver stops producing bile salts entirely during the first trimester
options.C: Bile stays in the gallbladder longer and becomes supersaturated with cholesterol
options.D: High iron supplements crystallize inside the biliary tree

explanation: When bile sits around too long and mixes with extra pregnancy cholesterol, it forms stones easily. Makes total sense when you think about it! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T4#GNS121_U7_T4_h5)

question: What happens to digestion when a woman goes into active labour?

options.A: It slows down significantly or stops almost entirely
options.B: It reverses direction, causing constant vomiting
options.C: It remains completely unchanged from normal pre-pregnancy rates
options.D: It speeds up to clear the body for delivery

explanation: The stress and pain of labour naturally put digestion on pause, meaning food stays in the stomach instead of moving along. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T4#GNS121_U7_T4_h6)

question: Why are women in active labour usually advised not to eat heavy solid foods?

options.A: To prevent sudden spikes in blood pressure during contractions
options.B: To keep the bowel completely empty to make room for the baby
options.C: To stop the stomach from producing excessive digestive acid
options.D: To prevent aspiration if vomiting occurs during delivery

explanation: Since food just sits in the stomach during labour, vomiting could cause stomach contents to slip into the lungs. Keeping meals light or restricted keeps mum safe! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T4#GNS121_U7_T4_h6)

question: What hormonal change helps the digestive tract get back to normal after childbirth?

options.A: A rapid drop in progesterone levels
options.B: A continuous high output of estrogen
options.C: A gradual increase in resting cortisol
options.D: A sudden surge in human placental lactogen

explanation: Once the placenta is delivered, progesterone levels drop fast, allowing the digestive tract to bounce right back to its normal tone. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T4#GNS121_U7_T4_h7)

question: What is a very common reason new mothers delay their first bowel movement after delivery?

options.A: Fear of pain from perineal stitches or hemorrhoids
options.B: Severe dehydration that dries out all body fluids
options.C: Complete lack of any urge to defecate for several weeks
options.D: Permanent paralysis of the colon caused by epidural anesthesia

explanation: Spot on. Soreness from stitches or swollen piles can make going to the toilet feel scary, so mums often hold back. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T4#GNS121_U7_T4_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT part of a routine check on a new mother's digestive recovery?

options.A: Asking when she last opened her bowels
options.B: Checking for bowel sounds and passage of gas
options.D: Inspecting the abdomen for signs of surgical wound breakdown

explanation: While surgical wound checks are vital after a C-section, general bowel recovery is all about checking for gas, bowel movements, and comfort down below. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T4#GNS121_U7_T4_h8)

question: A mum on her second day after delivery hasn't passed stool and is scared to use the toilet. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Withhold all oral fluids and food until she passes flatus
options.B: Administer a strong stimulant enema immediately without consulting a doctor
options.C: Insist that she remains in bed until her bowel movement happens naturally
options.D: Encourage fluid intake, walking around, and check if stool softeners were ordered

explanation: Gentle movement, plenty of fluids, and stool softeners are the safest, kindest way to help her first postpartum toilet trip go smoothly! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T4#GNS121_U7_T4_h8)

question: Which hormone relaxes the muscles of the urinary tract during pregnancy, causing the ureters to widen?

options.B: Prolactin

explanation: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscles all over the body. During pregnancy, this causes the tubes carrying urine from the kidneys to widen. You've got this! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h1)

question: Why is swelling of the kidney drainage system (hydronephrosis) more common on the right side during pregnancy?

options.A: The right renal artery has a higher pressure than the left.
options.B: The pregnant uterus tilts and compresses the right ureter more.
options.C: The right kidney is anatomically larger than the left kidney.
options.D: Progesterone receptors are concentrated only in the right ureter.

explanation: The growing uterus tends to lean to the right, putting extra pressure on the right ureter. Small details like this make you a sharp clinical nurse! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h1)

question: What usually happens to the rate at which the kidneys filter blood (GFR) during a normal pregnancy?

options.A: It increases by about fifty percent.
options.B: It drops sharply during the third trimester.
options.D: It decreases by about fifty percent.

explanation: Your kidneys work overtime during pregnancy, filtering blood at a much higher rate to handle waste for both mum and baby. Amazing how the body adapts! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h2)

question: At 20 weeks pregnant, a patient's serum creatinine level is 1.0 mg/dL. What does this result suggest?

options.B: Normal kidney function for pregnancy

explanation: Because kidney filtration speeds up during pregnancy, normal creatinine levels actually drop below 1.0 mg/dL. A value of 1.0 mg/dL means the kidneys might not be clearing waste as well as they should right now. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h2)

question: How can pregnant women hold onto extra water and sodium without their blood pressure shooting up?

options.A: Renal tubules stop working completely in the second trimester.
options.B: The heart pumps with a much weaker force.
options.C: Excess fluid is immediately stored in the amniotic sac.
options.D: Systemic vascular resistance decreases at the same time.

explanation: Blood vessels relax and widen during pregnancy, giving the extra fluid plenty of room so blood pressure stays nice and stable. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h3)

question: How do the kidneys balance out the mild breathing changes (respiratory alkalosis) that happen during pregnancy?

options.A: By excreting more bicarbonate in the urine
options.B: By shutting down the production of red blood cells
options.C: By storing extra carbon dioxide in the renal pelvis
options.D: By absorbing more sodium from the renal tubules

explanation: To keep the body's acid-base balance just right when a mum breathes a bit faster, the kidneys simply let go of some extra bicarbonate in the urine. Brilliant teamwork by the body systems! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h3)

question: What is a main reason why women struggle to pass urine during or right after childbirth?

options.A: High concentration of glucose in the urine
options.B: Pressure of the foetal head on the bladder neck
options.C: Sudden complete shutdown of the glomeruli

explanation: As the baby moves down the birth canal, the head can temporarily press on and block the urethra, making it hard to empty the bladder. Totally normal to encounter in labor wards! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h4)

question: Why might a woman with an epidural during labor not realize her bladder is getting too full?

options.B: Rapid increase in serum creatinine

explanation: An epidural numbs the lower body nerves, so the normal feeling of needing to pee is blocked. That's why midwives always check and help drain the bladder! Keep this in mind for your clinical postings. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h4)

question: What do we call the large amount of urine passed in the first few days after having a baby?

options.B: Glomerular shutdown

explanation: Postpartum diuresis is just the body's way of getting rid of all that extra pregnancy fluid it doesn't need anymore. Frequent trips to the bathroom are expected! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h5)

question: Why are new mums at high risk for their bladders getting overly full right after birth?

options.A: Decreased bladder sensation and birth trauma
options.B: Complete failure of the ureters to drain urine
options.C: High levels of circulating oxytocin in the blood
options.D: A sudden permanent drop in glomerular filtration

explanation: Swelling around the birth area and lingering numbness can trick the bladder, making it hard to empty fully. Good nursing care means keeping a close eye on this! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h5)

question: Four hours after a normal vaginal delivery, a mum hasn't peed yet, and her uterus feels soft (boggy) and pushed to the right. What is likely happening?

options.A: Sudden kidney failure caused by blood loss
options.B: A full bladder preventing the uterus from contracting
options.C: Normal postpartum diuresis filling the renal pelvis
options.D: Severe dehydration leading to low urine production

explanation: A full bladder acts like a roadblock, pushing the uterus out of place and stopping it from contracting properly. Always check the bladder if you notice a boggy uterus—it can prevent postpartum hemorrhage! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h6)

question: Why do midwives test pregnant women's urine with a dipstick for protein at every antenatal visit?

options.A: To help screen for early signs of preeclampsia
options.B: To measure the exact glomerular filtration rate
options.C: To check if the mother is drinking enough water
options.D: To confirm the presence of a normal twin pregnancy

explanation: Protein in the urine combined with high blood pressure is an early warning sign of preeclampsia. Routine dipsticks are a simple, life-saving tool in antenatal care! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T5#GNS121_U7_T5_h6)

question: Which two hormones easily cross into the brain to cause changes during pregnancy?

options.B: Estrogen and progesterone

explanation: You're doing great! Estrogen and progesterone rise during pregnancy and directly target brain receptors to help shape those new maternal feelings. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h1)

question: What is the main reason the brain undergoes structural changes during pregnancy?

options.A: To prepare the mother for caregiving and protect the baby
options.B: To slow down metabolic rates and prevent physical exhaustion
options.C: To permanently reduce the overall cognitive capacity of the woman
options.D: To compensate for a temporary lack of oxygen in the brain

explanation: It's fascinating how nature works! These brain changes help fine-tune maternal behavior and build emotional strength for looking after the little one. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h1)

question: Which temporary change happens to the maternal brain during pregnancy?

options.A: The permanent destruction of frontal lobe neurons
options.B: An increase in overall brain weight and skull size
options.C: A complete cessation of electrical wave activity
options.D: A temporary reduction in gray matter volume

explanation: Don't worry, moms aren't losing brain power! Gray matter dips slightly as the brain smartly reorganizes its neural networks for parenting. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h2)

question: Why do some pregnant women notice blurry vision or discomfort with contact lenses?

options.A: Retinal detachment occurs in every normal pregnancy
options.B: Fluid retention causes thickening of the cornea
options.C: High blood pressure damages the optic nerve directly
options.D: Extreme fatigue prevents the pupils from dilating

explanation: Spot on! Holding extra fluid during pregnancy can slightly change the shape and thickness of the cornea, which affects how light focuses. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h2)

question: What natural pain-relieving substance does the body release in large amounts during labour?

options.B: Beta-endorphins

explanation: The body is brilliantly designed! Beta-endorphins act as natural painkillers during labour by binding to special receptors in the nervous system. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h3)

question: How does the sympathetic nervous system react during active labour?

options.A: It stops breathing movements to rest the diaphragm
options.B: It lowers body temperature to conserve cellular fuel
options.C: It shuts down all sensory perception to force sleep
options.D: It increases heart rate, blood pressure, and energy output

explanation: Think of the 'fight-or-flight' response! It kicks in during labour to give the body the extra energy and push it needs for delivery. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h3)

question: What triggers the sudden mood swings and emotional shifts right after childbirth?

options.A: The total exhaustion of red blood cells in the brain
options.B: An abnormal buildup of carbon dioxide in brain tissue
options.C: A sudden increase in thyroid hormone production by the liver
options.D: The rapid drop in placental hormones like estrogen and progesterone

explanation: You've got this! Delivering the placenta causes a sudden drop in hormones, which can temporarily rock the nervous system and cause emotional ups and downs. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h4)

question: Which hormone stays high after childbirth to help the mother produce breast milk?

options.B: Aldosterone

explanation: Well done! Every time the baby suckles, prolactin surges to keep the milk flowing and support early nursing. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h4)

question: Which symptom is a classic warning sign of dangerous preeclampsia getting worse?

options.B: Severe frontal headache and hyperreflexia
options.C: Total loss of hearing in both ears
options.D: Sudden uncontrollable shaking of the feet

explanation: Always look out for this in clinicals! Brain irritation from high blood pressure and swelling often shows up as a bad headache and jumpy reflexes. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h5)

question: What is the main reason pregnant women get carpal tunnel syndrome in the third trimester?

options.A: A sudden tumor growth inside the carpal tunnel space
options.B: Permanent calcium deficiency destroying the bones of the wrist
options.C: Severe inflammation caused by repetitive typing work
options.D: Fluid retention causing tissue swelling that compresses the median nerve

explanation: Extra body fluid in late pregnancy swells the tissues inside the tight wrist space, pressing on the median nerve. Simple as that! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h5)

question: As a nurse, which quick bedside check helps detect nervous system irritability in a pregnant patient?

options.A: Listening for bowel sounds in all four quadrants
options.B: Testing the sense of taste and smell
options.D: Measuring the circumference of the skull

explanation: Checking reflexes is a quick, non-invasive way to spot nervous system irritation, especially when monitoring for preeclampsia. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h6)

question: A new mum is worried about being very forgetful two weeks after giving birth. What should you do?

options.A: Refer her immediately for a complex magnetic resonance imaging scan of the brain
options.B: Notify the primary physician that she is showing signs of early-onset dementia
options.C: Instruct her to stop breastfeeding immediately to restore normal vitamin levels
options.D: Reassure her that temporary cognitive shifts and memory lapses are normal adaptive changes

explanation: Be her comfort! Postpartum 'brain fog' is totally normal as the brain adjusts. Reassuring her goes a long way in easing her anxiety. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T6#GNS121_U7_T6_h6)

question: What is the primary maternal function of human chorionic gonadotropin in early pregnancy?

options.A: To stimulate milk production in maternal breast tissue
options.B: To lower maternal blood pressure for fetal protection
options.C: To trigger the immediate onset of active labour contractions
options.D: To stimulate the corpus luteum to produce progesterone

explanation: hCG signals the corpus luteum to keep producing progesterone early on, which protects and maintains the uterine lining until the placenta can take over that job. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h1)

question: How does human placental lactogen primarily help the developing fetus?

options.A: By directly oxygenating fetal blood within the intervillous space
options.B: By altering maternal metabolism to make more glucose available
options.C: By preventing maternal antibodies from attacking fetal tissues
options.D: By lubricating the birth canal in preparation for vaginal delivery

explanation: Placental lactogen acts as an antagonist to maternal insulin, ensuring that glucose stays in the bloodstream longer so it can readily cross over to nourish the fetus. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h1)

question: Why does the anterior pituitary gland enlarge during normal pregnancy?

options.A: Enlargement due to retained fluid volume
options.B: Proliferation of prolactin-secreting cells
options.C: Hypertrophy of cells producing growth hormone
options.D: Increased storage of oxytocin for delivery

explanation: The anterior pituitary grows noticeably larger because the cells that produce prolactin multiply rapidly to prepare the mother's body for breastfeeding. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of increased maternal aldosterone production during gestation?

options.A: To maintain a high level of urinary calcium excretion
options.B: To directly stimulate smooth muscle contractions in the uterus
options.C: To prevent dangerous spikes in maternal blood pressure
options.D: To help manage the large expansion of maternal blood volume

explanation: Elevated aldosterone encourages the kidneys to retain sodium and water, which supports the necessary increase in total blood volume needed to supply the placenta. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h2)

question: Why does the pregnant body develop normal insulin resistance during later gestation?

options.A: To protect maternal pancreatic beta cells from exhaustion and burnout
options.B: To encourage maternal fat storage for recovery after childbirth
options.C: To lower maternal blood pressure and prevent gestational hypertension
options.D: To ensure a steady supply of circulating glucose remains available for the fetus

explanation: Gestational insulin resistance makes maternal cells less sensitive to insulin, keeping more glucose in the blood so it can readily transfer across the placenta to the baby. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h3)

question: What happens to total maternal serum calcium levels during a normal pregnancy?

options.A: They decrease due to hemodilution and lower albumin
options.B: They increase significantly to support fetal bone growth
options.C: They remain completely unchanged throughout all trimesters
options.D: They drop dangerously low because of kidney failure

explanation: Total serum calcium drops because blood volume expands and blood protein levels fall, but ionized calcium stays normal. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h3)

question: What is the primary role of progesterone during the majority of a normal pregnancy?

options.A: To maintain uterine muscle relaxation and prevent early contractions
options.B: To trigger the posterior pituitary gland to release large amounts of oxytocin
options.C: To actively stimulate the frequent ripening of the uterine cervix
options.D: To raise maternal blood glucose levels for the growing fetus

explanation: Progesterone acts as a relaxant on the smooth muscle of the uterus, keeping it quiet and preventing premature labour throughout gestation. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h4)

question: How do local prostaglandins contribute to the process of childbirth?

options.A: By rapidly lowering maternal blood pressure to reduce hemorrhage risk
options.B: By blocking oxytocin receptors to give the uterus brief rest periods
options.C: By stopping the placenta from producing any more progesterone
options.D: By promoting cervical ripening and enhancing uterine contractions

explanation: Prostaglandins work locally in the pelvis to soften and dilate the cervix while also boosting the strength and frequency of uterine contractions. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h4)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding?

options.B: Oxytocin

explanation: Oxytocin causes the tiny muscles around the milk glands to contract, squeezing the milk out into the ducts for the baby. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h5)

question: Why does exclusive breastfeeding often delay the return of normal menstrual periods?

options.A: The placenta continues to secrete high amounts of progesterone postpartum
options.B: High prolactin levels suppress the release of GnRH from the hypothalamus
options.C: Estrogen levels remain permanently depleted while nursing an infant
options.D: The maternal ovaries completely shut down and atrophy after delivery

explanation: Frequent suckling keeps prolactin levels high, which suppresses the release of hypothalamic releasing hormones that stimulate ovulation. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h5)

question: A postpartum patient who delivered 24 hours ago asks why her blood sugar levels have suddenly dropped back to normal after needing insulin during pregnancy. What is the nurse's best response?

options.A: It is a sign that your kidneys are working too hard to filter extra sugar out of your blood.
options.B: The hormones from the placenta that caused insulin resistance were delivered with the baby.
options.C: This drop is only temporary and your blood sugar will spike again once your milk comes in.
options.D: Your pancreas has suddenly regenerated new cells to process all the sugar in your diet.

explanation: Once the placenta is expelled, the hormones causing gestational insulin resistance vanish, leading to an immediate drop in insulin requirements. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard nursing consideration related to postpartum endocrine changes?

options.A: Monitoring for sudden increases in maternal blood pressure caused by rising placental hormone levels
options.B: Observing for successful milk let-down reflex stimulated by infant suckling and oxytocin
options.C: Reassuring the mother about normal physiological changes during her hospital recovery
options.D: Assessing for signs of postpartum mood changes linked to rapid estrogen and progesterone withdrawal

explanation: Placental hormone levels drop rapidly after delivery, not rise. Therefore, rising placental hormone levels are not a concern postpartum. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T7#GNS121_U7_T7_h6)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for remodeling collagen and softening ligaments during pregnancy?

options.B: Insulin

explanation: Relaxin is produced during pregnancy to soften ligaments and joints, preparing the pelvis for delivery. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h1)

question: Why does joint looseness during pregnancy make women more prone to muscle or joint injury?

options.A: It causes rapid and uncontrolled bone growth in limbs.
options.B: It reduces joint stability across the entire skeletal system.
options.C: It stops bones from absorbing necessary dietary calcium.
options.D: It decreases the overall strength of muscle fibers.

explanation: When ligaments become loose, joints lose their normal tight support. This makes them much more prone to strain and injury during everyday tasks. You've got this! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h1)

question: In which direction does a pregnant woman's center of gravity shift as her uterus grows?

options.B: Backward

explanation: The growing uterus and fetus pull the body's weight forward, forcing the mother to adjust her posture to avoid falling. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h2)

question: How does the body naturally balance out the forward pull of a growing belly?

options.A: By leaning the upper torso and shoulders backward
options.B: By increasing the calcium density in the lower leg bones
options.C: By shortening the overall length of the spinal column
options.D: By bending the knees forward at all times

explanation: Leaning backward helps the mother keep her balance over her feet, though it places extra stress on the back muscles. Think of it as a natural balancing act! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h2)

question: What is the medical term for the exaggerated inward curve of the lower back seen in pregnancy?

options.B: Compensatory lumbar lordosis

explanation: Lordosis is just the natural inward curve of the lower back. During pregnancy, it becomes more pronounced (exaggerated) to help balance out the heavy bump. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h3)

question: A pregnant patient complains of severe lower back ache after standing for hours at her market stall. What is the main cause?

options.A: Inflammation of the bone marrow inside the vertebrae
options.B: Early degeneration of the spinal discs from calcium loss
options.C: Direct pressure of the fetal head on the lumbar nerves
options.D: Fatigue of the lower back muscles due to exaggerated spinal curves

explanation: The muscles along the lower spine have to work overtime to keep the body upright against the forward pull of pregnancy, leading to tiredness and aches. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h3)

question: Which specific pelvic joint is most directly affected by symphysis pubis dysfunction?

options.B: The hip socket joint

explanation: Symphysis pubis dysfunction causes pain right at the front pubic joint where the two pelvic bones meet. It's a common area of discomfort! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h4)

question: Which everyday activity is most likely to trigger sharp pain in a pregnant woman with relaxed pelvic joints?

options.A: Deep breathing exercises while sitting upright
options.B: Chewing hard foods during breakfast
options.C: Writing notes with a heavy pen
options.D: Stepping out of a car with one leg at a time

explanation: Movements that involve stepping out sideways or widening the legs unevenly—like getting out of a car—put extra strain on relaxed pelvic joints. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h4)

question: What is the classic description of the walking pattern often seen in late pregnancy?

options.B: An unsteady staggering gait

explanation: Pregnant women naturally widen their stance and swing their hips slightly more to maintain balance over relaxed joints and a heavy abdomen. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h5)

question: Why do pregnant women often develop swollen ankles and feet by the end of the day?

options.A: Arterial pressure in the legs drops to zero when sitting down.
options.B: Kidneys stop filtering water entirely during the third trimester.
options.C: The bones in the feet expand to make room for extra weight.
options.D: The growing uterus slows down blood return from the lower legs.

explanation: Pressure from the heavy uterus on the large blood vessels in the abdomen slows down blood flow coming back up from the legs, causing fluid to pool in the feet. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h5)

question: What happens to the pelvic joints to help the baby pass through the birth canal during labor?

options.A: They yield and allow slight widening of the pelvic ring.
options.B: They lock firmly in place to protect the spinal cord.
options.C: They shrink in size to push the baby downward.
options.D: They temporarily fuse into a single solid bone.

explanation: Relaxed pelvic ligaments let the bones shift slightly, creating a bit more space for the baby to move safely through the pelvis. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h6)

question: A nurse is positioning a woman on the delivery bed for a long second stage of labor. What action helps protect her joints?

options.A: Elevating the head of the bed to a complete vertical sitting position
options.B: Ensuring proper joint alignment and adding supportive padding
options.C: Tying the legs tightly together to prevent excessive spreading
options.D: Massaging the calf muscles vigorously every five minutes

explanation: Proper body alignment and extra padding prevent unnatural twisting on relaxed ligaments during long periods in awkward positions. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h6)

question: What is the term for the separation of the front abdominal wall muscles that often happens during pregnancy?

options.B: Carpal tunnel

explanation: Diastasis recti is simply the parting of the large front abdominal muscles to make room for the growing uterus. A very common finding in midwifery! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h7)

question: Why are new mothers still at risk for joint injuries in the weeks right after giving birth?

options.A: The sudden loss of body weight makes the skeleton extremely brittle.
options.B: New mothers stop using their muscles entirely while resting.
options.C: Relaxin hormone remains in the body for some time, keeping joints lax.
options.D: Breastfeeding draws all the calcium out of the arm and leg bones.

explanation: Even though delivery is done, relaxin takes several weeks to completely clear out of the bloodstream, leaving ligaments loose and vulnerable. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h7)

question: How does sleeping on the side with a pillow between the knees help a pregnant woman with back pain?

options.A: It prevents fluid from pooling in the upper body and arms.
options.B: It keeps the pelvis aligned and reduces twisting stress on the lower back.
options.C: It increases the amount of calcium absorbed by the spinal bones.
options.D: It completely stops the baby from moving around during the night.

explanation: Placing a pillow between the knees prevents the top leg from pulling the spine into an awkward twist while resting. Simple and effective advice for patients! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h8)

question: A nurse is teaching an antenatal class about preventing back strain. Which advice is best to share?

options.A: Lie flat on your back for long periods during the day to rest your spine.
options.B: Bend at your knees and keep loads close to your body when lifting objects.
options.C: Wear high-heeled shoes daily to strengthen your calf and ankle muscles.
options.D: Avoid all forms of physical activity until after the baby is born.

explanation: Good body mechanics—like lifting with the legs instead of the back—protect the vulnerable spine from unnecessary strain. Great teaching point! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h8)

question: What is the main hormone behind most skin changes during pregnancy?

options.B: Decreased cortisol levels

explanation: You've got this! High levels of pregnancy hormones like estrogen and progesterone wake up pigment cells and blood vessels in the skin. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h1)

question: Why do most pregnancy skin changes need no medical treatment?

options.A: Maternal skin becomes completely immune to disease
options.B: The placenta blocks all medications from working
options.C: Hormones stop circulating after the first trimester
options.D: They are normal body responses that fade after delivery

explanation: No stress here! Changes like darkening skin are just harmless body responses to pregnancy hormones that naturally get better after birth. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h1)

question: What is the dark vertical line that often appears on a pregnant belly called?

options.B: Striae gravidarum

explanation: Great job! Linea nigra simply means 'black line' in Latin—it's that common dark stripe that shows up on the tummy due to extra skin pigment. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h2)

question: A pregnant patient asks how to reduce dark patches on her face. What is the best nursing advice?

options.A: Scrub the face vigorously with harsh soap twice a day
options.B: Stop drinking milk immediately to clear skin pigment
options.C: Apply strong bleaching creams prescribed over the counter
options.D: Apply daily sunscreen and wear wide-brimmed hats outdoors

explanation: Sunlight makes facial darkening (melasma) pop out more. Advising sun protection is a simple, effective tip every nursing student should know! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h2)

question: What causes stretch marks, or striae gravidarum, during pregnancy?

options.A: Fungal infections growing under tight clothing
options.B: Blockage of sweat glands by high hormone levels
options.C: Accumulation of excess subcutaneous fat deposits
options.D: Breaking of elastic fibers in the dermis from rapid stretching

explanation: As the belly grows quickly, the elastic fibers in the deeper skin layer stretch and tiny breaks happen, leading to stretch marks. Completely normal! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h3)

question: Which finding is a normal vascular change expected during a routine prenatal checkup?

options.B: Small spider angiomas on the upper chest
options.C: Painful deep purple nodules on the calves
options.D: Complete absence of blood flow to the fingers

explanation: Spotting small spider-like blood vessels (angiomas) is super common due to extra blood volume and high estrogen during pregnancy. Nothing to worry about! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h3)

question: Why do many women experience sudden hair loss a few months after giving birth?

options.A: Breastfeeding drains all essential proteins from the scalp
options.B: Stored-up hairs from the growth phase shed all at once as hormones drop
options.C: Washing hair too frequently damages the weak hair roots
options.D: Newborn care stress permanently destroys hair follicles

explanation: During pregnancy, thick hormones hold onto your hair. Once those hormones drop after birth, all that extra hair decides to take a break and shed at once! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h4)

question: What is the term for the normal, temporary hair shedding that happens after childbirth?

options.B: Alopecia areata universalis

explanation: Fancy name, simple meaning! 'Telogen effluvium' just describes that normal phase where hair sheds after delivery before the cycle resets. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h4)

question: Which symptom is a major red flag for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy?

options.A: Painful blisters forming exclusively around the mouth
options.B: Rapid darkening of the skin over the entire body
options.C: Severe itching on the palms and soles without an initial rash
options.D: Thick crusting sores spreading across the scalp

explanation: Take note of this one for the ward! Intense itching on hands and feet without a rash can mean liver acid backup (cholestasis) and needs quick medical attention. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h5)

question: Which of these skin conditions needs careful medical evaluation rather than just reassurance?

options.A: Mild palmar erythema on the hands
options.B: Linea nigra across the lower abdomen
options.D: Spider angiomas on the upper chest

explanation: While lines and spider veins are harmless, cholestasis involves the liver and requires close monitoring to keep the baby safe. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h5)

question: What usually happens to stretch marks over time after delivery?

options.A: They fade from reddish-purple to silvery-white lines
options.B: They develop painful open ulcers that require suturing
options.C: They turn dark brown and raise above the skin surface
options.D: They completely disappear without leaving any trace

explanation: Stretch marks start out bright and angry-looking, but over time they calm down and fade into soft, silvery lines. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h6)

question: How does the body get rid of extra fluid from the skin and tissues right after birth?

options.A: Through rapid shedding of the top layer of skin cells
options.B: By reabsorbing all fluid directly back into the digestive tract
options.C: Through heavy postpartum sweating and increased urination
options.D: By storing extra fluid permanently in the muscle tissue

explanation: Sweating buckets and frequent bathroom trips are your body's clever ways of clearing out all that extra pregnancy fluid! [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h6)

question: A pregnant woman is worried about dark patches on her face and a line on her belly. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Reassure her that these are normal hormonal changes that usually fade after birth
options.B: Advise her to scrub the dark areas hard with soap every morning
options.C: Explain that these marks indicate a dangerous vitamin deficiency in her diet
options.D: Tell her to immediately see a dermatologist for emergency skin surgery

explanation: A warm, reassuring word goes a long way! Explaining that these marks are normal helps anxious mums relax. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h7)

question: What is a key nursing duty when checking a pregnant patient's skin?

options.A: Differentiating harmless body changes from serious medical conditions
options.B: Telling the patient to ignore any skin changes until after delivery
options.C: Reporting all common stretch marks to the primary surgeon
options.D: Prescribing strong steroid creams to cure all rashes instantly

explanation: You are the frontline! Knowing the difference between normal pregnancy glow-ups and warning signs like cholestasis makes you an awesome nurse. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h7)

question: What is the main chemical messenger used by the endocrine system?

options.B: Electrolytes

explanation: Spot on! Endocrine glands release hormones straight into the bloodstream to help regulate how different parts of the body work. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h1)

question: How does endocrine signaling mostly differ from the nervous system?

options.A: Endocrine organs use ducts to release chemicals.
options.B: Nervous responses use hormones instead of electricity.
options.C: Endocrine responses are slower and last longer.
options.D: Nervous signals target every cell in the body at once.

explanation: You got it! While nervous system signals flash by in a split second, endocrine signals travel through the blood and take their time to create lasting effects. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which part of the brain is the main bridge between the nervous and endocrine systems?

options.B: Thalamus

explanation: That's correct! The hypothalamus acts as the chief coordinator, linking brain signals to hormone control. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is a key difference between the anterior and posterior pituitary lobes?

options.A: The anterior lobe releases oxytocin into the bloodstream.
options.B: The anterior lobe ignores signals from the hypothalamus.
options.C: The posterior lobe produces growth hormone directly.
options.D: The posterior lobe only stores hormones made by the hypothalamus.

explanation: Well done! Think of the posterior pituitary as a warehouse—it doesn't make oxytocin or ADH itself, it just stores and releases them. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which gland releases a hormone to raise blood calcium when it drops too low?

options.B: Thyroid gland

explanation: Spot on! The tiny parathyroid glands step in with parathyroid hormone to pull calcium back into the blood when levels fall. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h3)

question: A patient with an underactive thyroid gland will most likely show which sign?

options.A: Changes in energy levels and metabolism
options.B: Rapid spikes in calcium-regulating hormones
options.D: Holding onto too much water with very little urine

explanation: That's right! The thyroid controls your body's engine speed, so when it slows down, the patient often feels sluggish and tired. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which hormone helps your body handle long-term stress?

options.B: Insulin

explanation: You nailed it! Cortisol is your body's main stress manager, helping you cope with physical and emotional pressure over time. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the main job of aldosterone from the adrenal glands?

options.A: Lowering blood sugar after a heavy meal
options.B: Helping bones grow during puberty
options.C: Making the heart beat faster during fright
options.D: Managing salt and water balance in the kidneys

explanation: Correct! Aldosterone tells your kidneys to hold onto sodium and water, which keeps your blood pressure steady. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which cells in the pancreas make insulin?

options.B: Acinar cells

explanation: Spot on! Beta cells in the pancreas are the ones responsible for producing insulin to bring your blood sugar down. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h5)

question: What happens in the body when alpha cells release glucagon into the bloodstream?

options.A: Insulin production stops completely in the pancreas.
options.B: Kidneys excrete large amounts of water and salt.
options.C: Body cells quickly absorb excess glucose from the blood.
options.D: The liver breaks down glycogen to raise low blood sugar.

explanation: Glucagon is released during fasting or low blood sugar states to stimulate glucose release from liver stores. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which gland produces melatonin to help control your sleep cycle?

options.B: Thyroid gland

explanation: That's correct! The pineal gland senses darkness and releases melatonin to help you wind down for sleep. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a main job of the gonads?

options.A: Quickly fixing sudden drops in blood pressure
options.B: Supporting secondary sex traits like body hair
options.D: Producing sex hormones like estrogen and testosterone

explanation: Spot on! Gonads focus on reproductive hormones. Blood pressure is managed by other organs like your kidneys and heart. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h6)

question: What type of feedback loop is most often used to keep hormone levels balanced?

options.B: Negative feedback

explanation: You nailed it! Negative feedback acts like a thermostat, turning hormone production up or down to keep things stable. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h7)

question: Why is knowing about negative feedback helpful in nursing care?

options.A: It proves hormones only work through nerves.
options.B: It explains why a struggling gland often causes the brain to pump out more stimulating hormones.
options.C: It means nurses never have to check lab results.
options.D: It keeps blood sugar high during exercise.

explanation: Brilliant! Because of negative feedback, if a target gland fails, the brain tries harder by sending out more stimulating hormones to compensate. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h7)

question: What is the main job of hormones in our bodies?

options.A: Generate fast electrical impulses for muscle movement
options.B: Fight off bacterial infections in the bloodstream
options.C: Digest food particles inside the stomach lumen
options.D: Act as chemical messengers to regulate body functions

explanation: Think of hormones as the body's postal service! They are chemical messengers sent out by glands to travel through the blood and help manage how different organs work. You've got this! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h1)

question: How does the endocrine system's signaling mainly differ from the nervous system?

options.A: Nervous signaling relies entirely on blood transport systems
options.B: Endocrine signaling uses fast electrical impulses directly to tissues
options.C: Nervous signaling controls long-term growth instead of rapid reflexes
options.D: Endocrine signaling is slower and provides longer-lasting control

explanation: While nerves give quick, snap reactions (like pulling your hand from fire), hormones take a bit longer to travel through the blood, but their effects stick around much longer. Great to know for clinical practice! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h1)

question: Which substance serves as the main chemical building block for steroid hormones?

options.B: Glucose

explanation: Steroid hormones are made straight from cholesterol! Even though people often talk about cholesterol in a bad nutritional light, our bodies actually need it to build vital hormones. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h2)

question: Why is it helpful for nurses to know a hormone's chemical structure?

options.A: It shows whether the hormone is made of white blood cells
options.B: It predicts how they travel in blood and interact with target cells
options.C: It dictates the exact caloric value of the hormone in the diet
options.D: It determines the exact time of day the gland will secrete them

explanation: Knowing whether a hormone is water-soluble or fat-soluble helps us understand how it moves through the blood and finds its target. Clinical pharmacology becomes much easier when you master this basics! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which amino acid is the starting point for making catecholamines and thyroid hormones?

options.B: Tyrosine

explanation: Tyrosine is the key building block amino acid used to manufacture important hormones like adrenaline and your thyroid hormones. One step at a time, you're learning it! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h3)

question: What makes thyroid hormones act a bit differently than other amino acid-derived hormones?

options.A: They are large proteins made of hundreds of linked amino acids
options.B: They only function within the nervous system as fast neurotransmitters
options.C: They cannot travel in the bloodstream without dissolving in red blood cells
options.D: They are fat-soluble and enter cells to bind intracellular receptors

explanation: Even though they start from an amino acid, thyroid hormones behave like fat-loving steroids—they slip right inside the cell to do their work. Tricky, but you'll never forget it now! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h3)

question: How do peptide and protein hormones typically travel through the bloodstream?

options.A: They require specialized carrier proteins to move through blood
options.B: They precipitate out of solution if not bound to electrolytes
options.C: They are water-soluble and dissolve freely in blood plasma
options.D: They are fat-soluble and travel inside red blood cells

explanation: Because protein and peptide hormones love water, they dissolve easily right into the watery plasma of your blood and swim along freely without needing a special ride. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h4)

question: Where do water-soluble peptide hormones usually find their target cell receptors?

options.A: On the outer surface of the target cell membrane
options.B: Attached to the outer wall of blood capillaries
options.C: Deep inside the nucleus of the target cell
options.D: Floating freely within the cytoplasm of the cell

explanation: Since water-soluble hormones can't cross the fatty cell membrane barrier, they have to knock on the front door by binding to receptors on the outside surface of the cell. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h4)

question: Which of these is a well-known example of a steroid hormone?

options.B: Cortisol

explanation: Cortisol is our classic stress steroid hormone, made by the adrenal cortex straight from cholesterol. You'll hear about cortisol constantly in medical-surgical nursing! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h5)

question: If a newly discovered hormone passes right through cell membranes without needing a surface receptor, what is it likely made of?

options.B: Water-soluble amine

explanation: Fat likes fat! Because steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, they slide smoothly across the fatty cell membrane to reach receptors inside. Brilliant deduction! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why do fat-soluble hormones need carrier proteins to travel in the blood?

options.A: Carrier proteins are needed to digest the hormone
options.B: They do not mix well with the watery plasma
options.C: They are too heavy to float without assistance
options.D: They would instantly destroy red blood cells if free

explanation: Oil and water don't mix! Since fat-soluble hormones don't dissolve in watery blood plasma, they need special carrier proteins to give them a ride through the circulatory system. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which portion of a fat-soluble hormone in the blood is actually active and able to affect cells?

options.A: The large fraction securely attached to liver carrier proteins
options.B: The small fraction that remains unbound or free in the blood
options.C: The portion that gets trapped inside blood vessel walls
options.D: The total amount secreted by the endocrine gland combined

explanation: Only the free, unattached hormones can slip out of the blood vessels to do their job. The rest stay safely hitched to their carrier proteins like passengers on a bus! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h6)

question: What system do water-soluble hormones use to pass along messages inside a cell?

options.B: Intracellular cholesterol

explanation: Since water-soluble hormones can't enter the cell themselves, they drop their message off at the surface, triggering a 'second messenger' inside the cell to carry out the orders. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h7)

question: Once a fat-soluble hormone gets inside a target cell, what is its main task?

options.B: Release calcium stores from the cell membrane
options.C: Regulate gene expression and protein synthesis
options.D: Block electrical impulses from the nervous system

explanation: Fat-soluble hormones go straight to the control center (the nucleus) to interact with DNA, turning specific genes on or off to make new proteins. You're crushing these physiology concepts! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h7)

question: Where do water-soluble hormones usually find their receptors?

options.B: Inside the cell nucleus

explanation: Because water-soluble hormones can't slip right through the oily cell membrane, they latch onto receptors sitting on the outside of the cell to pass their message along! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h1)

question: What happens right after a hormone hooks up with its target receptor?

options.A: A cascade of chemical messages is triggered inside the cell
options.B: The hormone is destroyed by the circulating antibodies
options.C: The cell membrane seals completely shut to block other signals
options.D: The cell immediately undergoes programmed cell death

explanation: Think of it like ringing a doorbell: once the hormone binds, it sets off an internal chain reaction that changes how the cell behaves and does its job. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h1)

question: Why would a cell decide to do receptor downregulation?

options.A: To help absorb more nutrients directly from the bloodstream
options.B: To protect itself from being overstimulated by high hormone levels
options.C: To prepare the cell to divide into two identical daughter cells
options.D: To allow fat-soluble hormones to cross the cell wall faster

explanation: If there's way too much hormone around for too long, the cell pulls some receptors inside to take a break and avoid getting overwhelmed. Smart cells know their limits! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h2)

question: If a patient's body has very low hormone levels for months, how will their target cells likely respond?

options.A: Receptor downregulation to conserve cellular energy
options.B: No change in receptor numbers on the cell membrane
options.C: Receptor upregulation to increase cellular sensitivity
options.D: Complete destruction of the hormone production glands

explanation: When hormones are scarce, cells put out more receptors—like putting out extra fishing nets—to catch every little bit of hormone that floats by. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is the main result when a genetic mutation affects a receptor?

options.A: The receptor becomes misshapen, altering normal hormone response
options.B: The hormone itself changes into a dangerous chemical toxin
options.C: The blood supply to the target endocrine gland is cut off
options.D: The cell membrane immediately dissolves into the bloodstream

explanation: A genetic typo changes the building blocks of the receptor protein, making its shape wonky so it doesn't fit the hormone key quite right. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h3)

question: How can a broken receptor cause health issues even if hormone levels are completely normal?

options.A: The excess hormone begins to crystallize inside the major organs
options.B: The immune system mistakes the healthy hormone for a foreign bacteria
options.C: The liver is forced to clear all circulating hormones too quickly
options.D: The target cells fail to respond or fire signals constantly without a trigger

explanation: Picture a broken lock: either the key won't turn at all, or the latch is stuck wide open and keeps firing signals when it shouldn't. Either way, trouble follows! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h3)

question: What hormone drives the growth of an ER-positive breast cancer tumor?

options.B: Insulin

explanation: ER stands for Estrogen Receptor! ER-positive tumors have these receptors on their surface and use estrogen like fuel to grow and multiply. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why do doctors test breast cancer tissue for HER2 receptors?

options.A: It tells the doctor exactly how many months the patient has to live
options.B: It prevents the cancer from spreading to the bone marrow
options.C: It proves the patient has a family history of endocrine disorders
options.D: It identifies tumors that may respond to specific HER2-blocking medications

explanation: Finding HER2 helps doctors target the cancer directly with specialized medications that block these specific growth signals. Modern medicine is amazing like that! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h4)

question: What is the main job of a receptor antagonist drug?

options.A: It converts water-soluble hormones into lipid-soluble molecules
options.B: It destroys all hormone-producing glands in the endocrine system
options.C: It binds to the receptor and blocks natural hormones from attaching
options.D: It forces the cell to produce twice as many receptors as normal

explanation: An antagonist is like a person sitting in a reserved cinema seat—they take up the spot so nobody else (no real hormone) can sit there. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h5)

question: How does a hormone agonist differ from a hormone antagonist?

options.A: An agonist triggers a cellular response, while an antagonist blocks it
options.B: An agonist destroys receptors, while an antagonist builds them
options.C: An agonist is taken orally, while an antagonist must be injected
options.D: An agonist only works on surface receptors, while antagonists work inside DNA

explanation: Agonists mimic the natural hormone and turn the pathway ON. Antagonists sit on the receptor and keep the pathway OFF. Easy to remember! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h5)

question: What does 'endocrine resistance' mean in cancer treatment?

options.A: When the liver breaks down medication too slowly to be effective
options.B: When the endocrine glands stop producing hormones permanently
options.C: When the patient's immune system attacks all circulating hormone pills
options.D: When tumor cells stop responding to a drug that once blocked their receptors

explanation: It's like cancer cells finding a loophole; even though the medication is blocking their usual path, the cancer figures out a way around it and keeps growing. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h6)

question: How do target cells commonly bypass receptor-blocking medications?

options.A: By dissolving the medication in the bloodstream using special enzymes
options.B: By activating alternative growth pathways that do not rely on the blocked receptor
options.C: By increasing the body's natural production of red blood cells
options.D: By reversing the mutation that caused the cancer in the first place

explanation: If the main front door is locked by drugs, clever cancer cells open up a side window (an alternate pathway) to keep getting what they need. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h6)

question: A patient taking an estrogen antagonist for breast cancer complains of hot flashes. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Document that the patient is allergic to the prescribed chemotherapy
options.B: Tell the patient to take extra birth control pills to replace the lost hormones
options.C: Advise the patient to stop taking the medication immediately because it is toxic
options.D: Explain that these symptoms often occur because the medication successfully blocks hormone receptors

explanation: Reassure your patient! Side effects like hot flashes happen because the drug is doing its job by blocking estrogen activity all over the body. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a core nursing responsibility for a patient on targeted receptor therapy?

options.A: Performing surgery to remove the endocrine glands
options.B: Providing emotional support for distressing physical side effects
options.C: Monitoring the patient closely for side effects related to hormone blockade
options.D: Educating the patient on the importance of taking medications regularly

explanation: Surgeons handle the operating room; nurses shine in assessment, patient education, emotional care, and managing side effects. You've got this! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the main difference between endocrine and exocrine glands?

options.A: Endocrine glands lack ducts and release hormones directly into the blood
options.B: Exocrine glands possess a rich network of fenestrated capillaries
options.C: Endocrine glands secrete substances exclusively onto the skin surface
options.D: Exocrine glands produce chemical messengers while endocrine glands do not

explanation: Think of endocrine glands as ductless delivery systems! Because they don't have tubes (ducts), they dump their hormones straight into the bloodstream to travel round the body. You've got this! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why are the tiny blood vessels (capillaries) inside endocrine glands specially built?

options.A: They lack endothelial linings to let whole secretory cells escape
options.B: They have thick walls to withstand high pressure from hormone surges
options.C: They are fenestrated to allow quick entry of hormones into the bloodstream
options.D: They contain valves that prevent the backflow of endocrine secretions

explanation: Fenestrated just means 'having tiny windows or pores'! These little pores make the capillary walls super leaky in a good way, helping hormones hop straight into your blood in no time. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h1)

question: Where does the front part of the pituitary gland (anterior pituitary) come from during early development?

options.A: The bony depression of the sphenoid bone known as the sella turcica
options.B: Downward growth of neural tissue directly from the hypothalamus
options.C: An outpouching of the embryonic pharynx called Rathke's pouch
options.D: The mesodermal layer surrounding the developing brain structures

explanation: Rathke's pouch is a fascinating little pocket of tissue from the roof of the mouth that pinches off to form the glandular front part of your pituitary. Embryology can look tricky, but breaking it down makes it simple! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the main functional difference between the front (anterior) and back (posterior) lobes of the pituitary gland?

options.A: The anterior lobe responds to nervous signals, while the posterior lobe responds exclusively to chemical blood signals
options.B: The anterior lobe synthesizes its own hormones, while the posterior lobe only stores and releases them
options.C: The posterior lobe produces releasing factors, while the anterior lobe targets the hypothalamus
options.D: The posterior lobe contains glandular epithelial cords, while the anterior lobe is made entirely of neurons

explanation: Remember: the anterior pituitary is a factory that makes its own hormones, while the posterior pituitary is more like a warehouse that just stores and sends out what the brain (hypothalamus) made for it! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the job of the jelly-like substance (colloid) found inside your thyroid gland?

options.A: To provide a rigid structural framework supporting the larynx
options.B: To manufacture parathyroid hormone for the posterior glands
options.C: To store thyroid hormone precursors until they are ready for release
options.D: To produce calcitonin for the regulation of blood calcium levels

explanation: Colloid acts like a storage warehouse inside the thyroid follicles, holding onto hormone building blocks safely until your body gives the signal to release them. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h3)

question: How can you tell parathyroid tissue apart from thyroid tissue under a microscope?

options.A: Parathyroid glands contain large amounts of colloid material for hormone storage
options.B: Parathyroid tissue is arranged in dense cords and nests rather than hollow follicles
options.C: Parathyroid glands lack blood capillaries within their parenchymal clusters
options.D: Parathyroid tissue is lined exclusively by ciliated columnar epithelial cells

explanation: While the thyroid forms hollow ring-like 'follicles' filled with jelly, the parathyroid packs its cells into neat little clusters and cords surrounded by tiny blood vessels. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which layer of the outer adrenal gland (adrenal cortex) produces stress hormones like cortisol?

options.B: Zona reticularis

explanation: Think of the adrenal cortex layers from outside in as Salt, Sugar, Sex (Glomerulosa, Fasciculata, Reticularis). The middle layer, zona fasciculata, handles the 'sugar' hormones like cortisol to help you cope with stress! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h4)

question: What type of cells make up the inner part of the adrenal gland (adrenal medulla), and where do they come from?

options.A: C cells derived from the embryonic pharyngeal pouches
options.B: Chromaffin cells, which are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons
options.C: Epithelial cells arranged in hollow spherical follicles containing colloid
options.D: Follicular cells that synthesize and store mineralocorticoids

explanation: The adrenal medulla is unique! Its chromaffin cells are basically modified nerve cells that release adrenaline straight into your blood during a fight-or-flight moment. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary job of the alpha cells in the pancreas (Islets of Langerhans)?

options.A: Releasing digestive enzymes into pancreatic ducts
options.B: Producing insulin to lower circulating blood sugar
options.C: Synthesizing somatostatin to inhibit neighboring cells
options.D: Secreting glucagon to raise blood glucose levels

explanation: Easy way to remember: Alpha = 'A'lways brings sugar up (glucagon), while Beta cells bring blood sugar down with insulin. You've got this nursing concept down! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why do we call the pancreas a 'heterocrine' (or mixed) organ?

options.A: It releases secretions into both lymphatic vessels and blood capillaries
options.B: Its structure combines neural tissue with glandular epithelial cords
options.C: It produces two opposing hormones, insulin and glucagon, from beta cells
options.D: It contains both exocrine digestive tissue and endocrine hormone-producing islets

explanation: The pancreas wears two hats! It acts as an exocrine gland by sending digestive juices through ducts to your gut, and an endocrine gland by releasing hormones like insulin straight into your blood. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which hormone is produced by the pineal gland in your brain?

options.B: Melatonin

explanation: Melatonin is your body's natural clock keeper! Released by the pineal gland when it gets dark, it helps signal to your body that it's time to sleep. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h6)

question: What happens to the thymus gland as a person grows older?

options.A: It accumulates calcified deposits known as corpora arenacea
options.B: Its pinealocytes transform entirely into hormone-secreting neurons
options.C: It develops hollow colloid-filled follicles similar to the thyroid
options.D: It undergoes fatty involution and gradually shrinks in size

explanation: As we age, the active immune tissue in the thymus slowly gets replaced by fat cells—a natural process called involution. Nothing to worry about, it's just part of normal aging! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which hormone is released by special cells in the heart when the heart walls get stretched too much?

options.B: Renin

explanation: When your heart chambers are stretched by high blood volume, they release Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) to tell your kidneys to get rid of extra water and salt, helping lower your blood pressure. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h7)

question: How do hormone-producing cells in the Diffuse Neuroendocrine System (DNES) differ from traditional glands?

options.A: They consist exclusively of modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons derived from neural crest tissue
options.B: They possess specialized ducts that empty their chemical secretions directly into the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract
options.C: They lack a blood supply entirely and rely purely on local nervous system stimulation for hormone distribution
options.D: Their hormone-producing cells are scattered singly among other mucosal cell types rather than clustered in a dedicated gland

explanation: Instead of sitting together in one organ (like the thyroid), DNES cells are scattered solo across places like your gut lining, quietly sending out local chemical signals. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is the main difference between endocrine and exocrine glands?

options.A: Endocrine glands lack ducts and secrete straight into the blood
options.B: Endocrine glands release sweat and digestive enzymes onto body surfaces
options.C: Exocrine glands use rich capillary networks instead of tubular ducts
options.D: Exocrine glands produce chemical messengers for distant target organs

explanation: Think of endocrine glands as being ductless—they pour their chemical messages directly into the bloodstream. Exocrine glands, like sweat glands, use tubes (ducts) to send their products to a body surface. You've got this! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h1)

question: What is the main job of the endocrine system in the body?

options.A: Filtering metabolic waste products out of circulating blood plasma
options.B: Directing immediate, split-second muscle movements and reflexes
options.C: Coordinating slow, sustained processes like growth and metabolism
options.D: Producing physical barriers to protect internal organs from pathogens

explanation: While your nervous system handles quick reflexes (like pulling your hand from a hot stove), the endocrine system takes the long view—slowly and steadily managing things like your growth, mood, and metabolism. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which group of hormones is made directly from cholesterol?

options.B: Steroid hormones

explanation: Steroid hormones are built using cholesterol as their base material. Because of this, they share a fat-loving (lipophilic) nature! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h2)

question: Why do steroid hormones need carrier proteins to travel through the blood?

options.A: Because carrier proteins protect them from being digested by blood enzymes
options.B: Because they are fat-soluble and do not dissolve well in water-based blood plasma
options.C: Because they are too large to fit through the walls of blood capillaries alone
options.D: Because carrier proteins are required to activate their chemical structure

explanation: Since blood is mostly water and steroid hormones are fat-based, they don't mix well on their own. Carrier proteins act like VIP transport vehicles to get them safely through the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the very first, inactive protein chain made from mRNA during peptide hormone production called?

options.B: A prohormone

explanation: Before a peptide hormone is ready, the cell makes a starter version called a preprohormone. It gets trimmed down step-by-step into the active hormone! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h3)

question: Where does a prohormone usually get turned into its final, active hormone form?

options.A: Inside secretory vesicles as they wait to be released
options.B: Directly on the surface of the rough endoplasmic reticulum
options.C: Inside the cell nucleus during the transcription of DNA
options.D: Out in the bloodstream after the molecule leaves the cell

explanation: The final cutting and polishing happens right inside the storage bubbles (secretory vesicles) as the cell waits for the signal to release the hormone. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h3)

question: Which parts of the cell contain the tools needed to turn cholesterol into steroid hormones?

options.B: Lysosomes and the cell plasma membrane
options.D: The cell nucleus and the Golgi apparatus

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! The mitochondria and the smooth endoplasmic reticulum team up to convert cholesterol into active steroid hormones. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why can steroid hormones slip right out of cells as soon as they are made?

options.A: They are pushed out by water pressure inside the cytoplasm
options.B: They are small enough to pass through active transport protein pumps
options.C: They are stored in large vesicles that burst open upon stimulation
options.D: They are fat-soluble and can cross lipid cell membranes easily

explanation: Because cell membranes are also made of fats (lipids), fat-loving steroid hormones pass straight through them like an open door—no special channels needed! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h4)

question: How do cells release stored peptide hormones into the fluid outside the cell?

options.B: Pinocytosis

explanation: Peptide hormones are packed in little bubbles that fuse with the cell membrane, popping open to spill their contents outside. That process is called exocytosis! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h5)

question: What must a cell do if it makes steroid hormones and suddenly receives a continuous call to release more?

options.A: It must rapidly synthesize new hormone molecules from cholesterol on the spot
options.B: It pumps stored hormones out of the cytoplasm using ATP energy channels
options.C: It opens storage vesicle gates to release a large backup supply of ready hormones
options.D: It stops producing hormones until old supplies are cleared from the blood

explanation: Unlike peptide hormones, steroid hormones aren't stored in large stockpiles. If the body needs more right now, the cell has to manufacture them fresh from cholesterol immediately. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is the body's main way of stopping hormone levels from climbing too high?

options.B: Receptor downregulation

explanation: Negative feedback is like a thermostat: when hormone levels get too high, a signal is sent to slow down production and bring things back to normal. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a positive feedback loop?

options.A: Insulin lowering blood glucose levels after a carbohydrate-rich meal
options.B: Cortisol suppressing the hypothalamus from releasing stress hormones
options.C: Oxytocin release intensifying uterine contractions during childbirth
options.D: Thyroid hormone stopping the release of thyroid-stimulating hormone

explanation: Positive feedback pushes a process even faster until the goal is met! Childbirth is a great example: oxytocin causes contractions, which trigger more oxytocin, until the baby is born. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h6)

question: What term is used for the time it takes for half of a hormone to be cleared from the bloodstream?

options.B: Metabolic rate

explanation: Just like medicine in the body, a hormone's 'half-life' is simply how long it takes for half of its concentration in the blood to disappear. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h7)

question: Which two organs do the heaviest lifting when it comes to breaking down and removing hormones?

options.B: Lungs and skin

explanation: Your liver chemically alters and breaks down used hormones, while your kidneys filter the leftovers out into your urine. Great tag-team work! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h7)

question: What word describes an endocrine gland producing way too much hormone?

options.B: Homeostasis

explanation: Break it down: 'hyper' means high or excessive, and 'secretion' means releasing a substance. So, hypersecretion means too much hormone output! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h8)

question: A patient has an autoimmune condition where their insulin-making cells are destroyed. What lab finding is most likely?

options.A: Dangerously low blood sugar caused by excess hormone release
options.B: Rapid weight gain due to slowed metabolic breakdown
options.C: Elevated blood glucose levels due to a lack of insulin
options.D: Increased water retention and high blood pressure

explanation: Without insulin (hyposecretion), glucose can't easily enter the body's cells to be used for energy. Instead, it builds up in the bloodstream, leading to high blood sugar. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h8)

question: What is the main job of hormones in our bodies?

options.A: Generate rapid electrical impulses for muscle contraction
options.B: Transport oxygen molecules from the lungs to body tissues
options.C: Filter waste products directly out of the bloodstream
options.D: Act as chemical messengers to regulate target organs

explanation: Think of hormones as chemical text messages sent through the blood to tell different organs what to do. You've got this! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h1)

question: How is endocrine signaling different from nervous system signaling?

options.A: Nervous signaling produces much slower, permanent bodily changes
options.B: Nervous signaling relies entirely on circulating blood vessels
options.C: Endocrine signaling uses direct physical contact with cells
options.D: Endocrine signaling is slower and has longer-lasting effects

explanation: Nerve impulses are like a quick flash of lightning, while hormones are like a slow, steady wave whose effects linger much longer. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which part of the brain connects the nervous system to the endocrine system?

options.B: Medulla oblongata

explanation: The hypothalamus is the master bridge! It takes messages from the brain and turns them into hormonal orders. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is the main job of the posterior pituitary gland?

options.A: It breaks down worn-out hormones in the bloodstream
options.B: It stores and releases hormones produced by the hypothalamus
options.C: It manufactures tropic hormones for the adrenal glands
options.D: It controls blood calcium levels using direct neural input

explanation: The posterior pituitary acts like a warehouse—it doesn't make hormones itself, but safely stores and releases them when needed. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h2)

question: What triggers hormone release during humoral stimulation?

options.A: Tropic hormones secreted by the anterior pituitary
options.B: Emotional stress and physical trauma responses
options.C: Changes in ion or nutrient levels in the blood
options.D: Direct electrical impulses sent from the brain

explanation: Humoral stimuli mean the glands are tasting the blood directly—like checking if there is too much sugar or calcium floating around. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h3)

question: A patient just ate a heavy meal loaded with carbs. What happens right away?

options.A: The parathyroid will secrete parathyroid hormone due to calcium shifts
options.B: The adrenal cortex will stop producing cortisol entirely
options.C: The pancreas will release insulin due to rising blood glucose
options.D: The hypothalamus will block all tropic hormone production

explanation: As sugar rises in the blood after eating, the pancreas senses it directly and releases insulin to bring it back down. Simple and smart! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h3)

question: Which gland gets a direct emergency signal from nerves during stress?

options.B: Parathyroid gland

explanation: When you get a sudden fright, the nervous system instantly triggers the adrenal medulla to pump out adrenaline for that fight-or-flight burst. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h4)

question: Why is it helpful for the body to use direct nerve control during sudden danger?

options.A: It relies entirely on blood nutrient concentration changes
options.B: It ensures long-term maintenance of blood calcium levels
options.C: It provides a much faster response than hormonal feedback loops
options.D: It prevents the pancreas from secreting too much insulin

explanation: When danger strikes, you don't have time to wait for slow chemical travel—nerves act in a split second to keep you safe! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the main goal of a negative feedback loop in the body?

options.A: To trigger rapid nerve impulses during acute physical pain
options.B: To maintain hormone levels within a stable, normal range
options.C: To continuously amplify hormone production until exhaustion
options.D: To replace lost nutrients in the extracellular fluid

explanation: Think of negative feedback like an air conditioner: when the room gets too cold (or hormone levels get too high), it turns things off to keep balance. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h5)

question: Which of these is a great example of a positive feedback loop?

options.A: Insulin lowering high blood sugar back to normal
